e.etymology: An English phonetic spelling of Juanita, the Spanish pet form of Juana, which is the feminine of Juan, or John.
An elaboration of Cora with the diminutive ending -etta. Cora goes back to Greek kore, maiden.
namesakes: Coretta Scott King (civil rights leader, wife of Martin Luther King Jr.)

assoc.t: Coretta Scott King, civil rights leader

e.etymology: Used mainly in Spanish-speaking families and grouped by name references with Abelia and Velia; its own source is not settled.
American use peaked in the late 1980s and looks like a modern coinage. Separately, Taja is a Slovene short form of Tatjana.
The feminine of Sophronius, from Greek sophron, self-controlled or sensible. It was in regular American use through the 19th century.
From Greek Parthenia, virginity, built on parthenos, maiden, the word behind the Parthenon. The name occurs in Greek mythology.
A surname used as a first name. The surname comes from Pate, an old Scots and northern English short form of Patrick, or from the Middle English word for the crown of the head.
e.note: On paper it can be read as pâté or as pate, the old word for the top of the head.

e.etymology: A spelling of Sheila, the English form of Irish Síle, which is the Irish version of Cecilia. Cecilia comes from a Roman family name built on caecus, blind.
A variant of Bernardine, a feminine form of Bernard, from Germanic words for bear and hardy.
A variant of Letitia, from Latin laetitia, gladness. It also fits the African-American tradition of names coined with La-.
A spelling of Miranda, which Shakespeare coined for The Tempest from Latin mirandus, worthy of admiration.
A spelling of Susan, from Hebrew Shoshannah, lily, by way of Greek and French. Suzan is also a regular spelling of the name in Turkey.
A short form of names ending in -lyn, such as Carolyn and Evelyn, and a pared-down spelling of Lynn.
An elaboration of Laura or Lauren with the ending -een. Both go back to Latin laurus, the laurel tree, by way of Laurentius.
A spelling of Katie, the pet form of Katherine. In Finland and Hungary Kati is the usual short form of Katariina and Katalin.
From a surname, a spelling of Wayman, taken up as a first name in the American South.
A short form or variant of Esther, the Biblical queen's name, usually traced to a Persian word for star.
From French Romain and its feminine Romaine, from Latin Romanus, Roman. English borrowed it as a given name and a surname, and in the United States it has been given mostly to boys.
e.note: Romaine is the everyday name of a lettuce, so expect salad jokes.

e.etymology: A spelling of Dean, a surname from Middle English dene, valley, or from the church office of dean. In Ireland Deane also anglicizes a Gaelic surname meaning son of the deacon.
A spelling of Lorraine, the name of a region of eastern France that took its name from the medieval kingdom of Lothar. The 1940s film star Laraine Day made this spelling familiar.
namesakes: Laraine Newman (original Saturday Night Live cast member)

e.etymology: Usually treated as a phonetic English form of Irish Sinéad, itself from French Jeannette. It also fits the Sha- names popular in the United States around 1990.
A spelling of Terence, from Terentius, a Roman family name of obscure origin borne by a Roman playwright and by early saints.
A variant of Marlena, an elaborated form of Marlene, the German blend of Maria and Magdalene.
A spelling of Anthony, from Antonius, a Roman family name of uncertain origin. The h crept in during the Renaissance from a mistaken link to Greek anthos, flower.
A respelling of Michael, from Hebrew Mikha'el, a rhetorical question meaning who is like God?
namesakes: Mychal Thompson (NBA champion and broadcaster, father of Klay Thompson)

e.etymology: Mary and Louise written as one name. Mary is the English form of Hebrew Miriam, and Louise is the French feminine of Louis.
namesakes: Mary-Louise Parker (actress in Weeds and Fried Green Tomatoes)

e.etymology: A pared-down spelling of Brittany, the English name of the Breton region of France, by way of Britney.
A spelling of Latifa, the feminine of Arabic Latif, gentle or kind.
A phonetic spelling of Giles, the medieval English form of a French saint's name that goes back to Greek aigidion, kid or young goat.
Not a name parents chose: a placeholder in US birth records for babies whose certificates were filed before a name was decided.
e.note: Appears in name statistics only as a record-keeping placeholder for babies not yet named.

e.etymology: A spelling of Sandra, the short form of Alessandra and Alexandra, from Greek alexo, to defend, and aner, man.
namesakes: Sondra Locke (actress and Clint Eastwood co-star)

e.etymology: The short form of Edward, Edgar, Edwin and Edmund, which all begin with Old English ead, wealth or good fortune.
namesakes: Ed Harris (actor in Apollo 13 and The Truman Show)

assoc.t: ED, the common abbreviation for erectile dysfunction
